'''Moses Judah Folkman''' (February 24, 1933 – January 14, 2008)<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://eye.hms.harvard.edu/judahfolkman |title=Judah Folkman, MD |website=Department of Ophthalmology |publisher=Harvard Medical School |access-date=February 18, 2019 }}</ref> was an American biologist and pediatric surgeon best known for his research on tumor [[angiogenesis]], the process by which a tumor attracts blood vessels to nourish itself and sustain its existence. He founded the field of angiogenesis research, which has led to the discovery of a number of therapies based on inhibiting or stimulating neovascularization.<ref name=PNAS2008>{{cite journal |author=Cao, Yihai |author2=Langer, Robert |author-link2=Robert S. Langer |title=A review of Judah Folkman's remarkable achievements in biomedicine |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |date=September 9, 2008 |volume=105 |issue=36 |pages=13203–13205 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0806582105 |pmc=2533169 |pmid=18772371 |bibcode=2008PNAS..10513203C|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Early life==
Born in 1933 in Cleveland, Ohio, Judah Folkman accompanied his father, a [[rabbi]] of [[Austrian-Jewish]] descent, on visits to hospital patients. By age seven, he knew he wanted to be a doctor rather than follow in his father's footsteps, so he could offer cures in addition to comfort. His father replied, "In that case, you can be a rabbi-like doctor," words his son took to heart.<ref name=RememberingCHB>Children's Hospital Boston [https://web.archive.org/web/20120210125621/http://www.childrenshospital.org/cfapps/research/data_admin/Site2580/mainpageS2580P1.html Remembering Judah Folkman: Biography]</ref>

Folkman graduated from [[Ohio State University]] in 1953, and then [[Harvard Medical School]] in 1957.<ref name="HarvardBIo">Harvard Medical School [https://fa.hms.harvard.edu/files/memorialminute_folkman_judah.pdf Bio at Harvard Medical School]</ref> While a student at Harvard Medical School, he trained under [[Robert Edward Gross]]<ref name="NASbio">[[Patricia K. Donahoe|Patricia K Donahoe]]. [https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/folkman-judah.pdf Judah Folkman: 1933–2008. A Biographical Memoir] National Academy of Sciences, 2014</ref> and also worked on a prototype [[Artificial cardiac pacemaker|pacemaker]], work that he never published.<ref name="AcadAchieve">Academy of Achievement. June 17, 2010 [http://www.achievement.org/autodoc/page/fol0bio-1 Judah Folkman Biography, Foundations for Cancer Therapy] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080119114953/http://www.achievement.org/autodoc/page/fol0bio-1|date=January 19, 2008}}</ref> 

In 1960, his residency was interrupted when he was drafted in the [[United States Navy]] and did research for the Navy until 1962 at the [[National Naval Medical Center]] in [[Bethesda, Maryland]].  During that time, he studied the use of [[silastic]] for the sustained release of [[lipophilic]] drugs; the 1964 publication of that work helped inspire the technological development of the [[Norplant]] implantable contraceptive at the [[Population Council]].<ref>Laura J. Frost and Michael R. Reich [http://www.accessbook.org/downloads/chapter_6_AccessBook.pdf Access: How Do Good Health Technologies Get to Poor People in Poor Countries?] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160212201148/http://www.accessbook.org/downloads/chapter_6_AccessBook.pdf|date=February 12, 2016}} Bibliomotion, Inc., 2014. {{ISBN|9781629560304}}</ref>{{rp|117}}<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Folkman J, Long DM |date=Mar 1964 |title=The Use of Silicone Rubber as a Carrier for Prolonged Drug Therapy |journal=J Surg Res |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=139–42 |doi=10.1016/s0022-4804(64)80040-8 |pmid=14130164}}</ref>

The navy research was focused on developing artificial blood; in the course of testing potential products to see if they could keep alive thymus glands taken from rabbits, he noticed that tumors in the gland could not grow as they did if the glands were perfused with blood.  His curiosity as to why led to his work on angiogenesis.<ref name="RememberingCHB" />

After his two years work for the navy, Folkman completed his residency at Massachusetts General Hospital.  He worked as an assistant surgeon at Boston City Hospital, then trained further in pediatric surgery at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia under [[C. Everett Koop]].<ref name="NASbio" />

==Career==
In 1967 he was appointed surgeon-in-chief of [[Children's Hospital Boston]] at the age of 34. Folkman was appointed the Julia Dyckman Andrus Professor of Pediatric Surgery at Harvard Medical School in 1968, where he was also Professor of Cell Biology. He was the youngest full Professor in the history of Harvard Medical School.<ref name="RememberingCHB" /> In addition to directing the Children's Hospital Boston Surgical Research Laboratories, which grew to become the Vascular Biology Program, for nearly four decades, he was the Scientific Director of the hospital's Vascular Anomalies Center.<ref name="RememberingCHB" />

In 1971, he reported in the ''[[New England Journal of Medicine]]'' that [[solid tumor]]s are [[angiogenesis]]-dependent.<ref name=NASbio/><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Folkman|first1=J|title=Tumor angiogenesis: therapeutic implications|journal=New England Journal of Medicine|date=1971|volume=285|issue=21|pages=1182–1186|doi=10.1056/NEJM197111182852108|pmid=4938153}}</ref>  He hypothesized that there was an unknown "factor" that tumors secreted to help it increase its blood supply, and that if that factor could be blocked, tumors would wither and die. Though his hypothesis was initially disregarded and treated with skepticism by most experts in the field, Folkman persisted with his research.<ref name=HarvardBIo/>  He and collaborators, who included [[Bert L. Vallee]], soon identified the already-known [[fibroblast growth factor]] as an angiogenic factor, but the team's work showed that there were additional, unknown factors.<ref name=PNAS2008/> To help accelerate the work, Folkman started collaborating with industry.<ref name=NASbio/> In 1974 Harvard University and [[Monsanto]] signed a ten-year [[Medical research#Privately .28industry.29 funded biomedical research|industrial-funded research grant]] to support his cancer research, which at that time was the largest such arrangement ever made; medical inventions arising from that research were the first for which Harvard allowed its faculty to submit a [[patent application]].<ref name=HarvardBIo/><ref name=NASbio/> [[Robert Langer]] worked as a postdoc in Folkman's lab during this time, concentrating on using [[silastic]] and other materials to deliver drugs.<ref name=NASbio/>

In the mid to late 1980s, two other angiogenic factors were identified by other labs that had been inspired by his work: [[angiogenin]] and [[VEGF]].<ref name=NASbio/> With the factors identified, [[drug discovery]] could begin. When the Monsanto agreement (which yielded no products for Monsanto) ended, Folkman started receiving research funding from [[Takeda Pharmaceutical Company|Takeda]] and then from a startup company, [[CASI_Pharmaceuticals|Entremed]], that put half its venture capital funding into research in the Folkman lab.<ref name=NASbio/>

[[Donald E. Ingber]] soon discovered that a fungus, ''[[Aspergillus fumigatus]]'', secreted a chemical, [[fumagillin]], that inhibited angiogenesis.  Takeda performed [[medicinal chemistry]] to optimize it, leading to development of TNP-470.<ref name=NASbio/> Folkman's team later tested it in adults with [[hemangiomas]]; they also used [[interferon alpha]], an already approved drug that they had already shown to be an angiogenesis inhibitor, to treat infants with hemangiomas in some of the first clinical trials of angiogenesis inhibitors which were published in 1992.<ref name=Beilenberg>{{cite journal | vauthors = Bielenberg DR, D'Amore PA | year = 2008 | title = Judah Folkman's contribution to the inhibition of angiogenesis | journal = Lymphat Res Biol. | volume = 6 | issue = 3–4| pages = 203–7 | doi = 10.1089/lrb.2008.1016 | pmid = 19093793 }}</ref> In these trials they also studied the levels of [[fibroblast growth factor]] in the urine of the trial subjects and published that work in 1994; these were some of the first explorations of the use of [[biomarkers]] in clinical trials as [[surrogate endpoints]].<ref name=NASbio/><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors = Nguyen M, Watanabe H, Budson AE, Richie JP, Hayes DF, Folkman J | title = Elevated levels of an angiogenic peptide, basic fibroblast growth factor, in the urine of patients with a wide spectrum of cancers | journal = J. Natl. Cancer Inst. | volume = 86 | issue = 5 | pages = 356–61 | date = March 1994 | pmid = 7508518 | doi = 10.1093/jnci/86.5.356 }}</ref>

In 1991 Michael O"Reilly, working in the Folkman lab with Entremed funding, discovered the first endogenous angiogenesis inhibitor, [[angiostatin]] and then another, [[endostatin]]. Entremed began developing them and soon struck a collaboration with [[Bristol-Myers]], which caught national interest and spurred further investment in angiogenesis inhibitors by other pharma companies.<ref name=NASbio/><ref name=Tribune>John Crewdson for the Chicago Tribune. April 11, 1999 [https://www.chicagotribune.com/1999/04/11/crucial-test-for-cancer-drug/ Crucial Test For Cancer Drug]</ref>

In 1993 he surprised the scientific world by hypothesizing that angiogenesis is as important in [[blood cancers]] as it is in solid tumors,<ref name=Folkman>{{cite journal | vauthors = Folkman J | date = Dec 2001 | title = Angiogenesis-dependent diseases | journal = Semin Oncol | volume = 28 | issue = 6| pages = 536–42 | pmid = 11740806 | doi=10.1016/s0093-7754(01)90021-1}}</ref> and the next year he published work showing that a [[biomarker]] of angiogenesis was higher in all people with cancer, but especially high in people with blood cancers, and other evidence of the role of angiogenesis in blood cancers emerged as well.<ref name=Folkman/> Meanwhile, a member of his lab, Robert D'Amato, was looking for [[angiogenesis inhibitors]], and discovered that [[thalidomide]] inhibited angiogenesis in 1994.<ref name="pmid7513432">{{cite journal | vauthors = D'Amato RJ, Loughnan MS, Flynn E, Folkman J | title = Thalidomide is an inhibitor of angiogenesis | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America | volume = 91 | issue = 9 | pages = 4082–4085 | year = 1994 | pmid = 7513432 | pmc = 43727 | doi = 10.1073/pnas.91.9.4082 | bibcode = 1994PNAS...91.4082D | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | pmc=2268723 | pmid=18247146 | doi=10.1007/s10456-008-9092-6 | volume=11 | title=Judah Folkman, a pioneer in the study of angiogenesis | year=2008 | journal=Angiogenesis | pages=3–10 | vauthors=Ribatti D| issue=1 }}</ref> Around that time, the wife of a man who was dying of multiple myeloma and whom standard treatments had failed, called Folkman asking him about his anti-angiogenesis ideas.<ref name=Beilenberg/> Folkman convinced the patient's doctor to try thalidomide, and that doctor ended up conducting a clinical trial of thalidomide for people with multiple myeloma in which about a third of the subjects responded to the treatment.<ref name=Beilenberg/> The results of that trial were published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1999.<ref name=Beilenberg/><ref name="nejm-myeloma">{{cite journal | vauthors = Singhal S, Mehta J, Desikan R, Ayers D, Roberson P, Eddlemon P, Munshi N, Anaissie E, Wilson C, Dhodapkar M, Zeddis J, Barlogie B | title = Antitumor activity of thalidomide in refractory multiple myeloma | journal = N. Engl. J. Med. | volume = 341 | issue = 21 | pages = 1565–71 | date = November 1999 | pmid = 10564685 | doi = 10.1056/NEJM199911183412102 | s2cid = 45150547 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

In 2004, the first angiogenesis inhibitor, [[bevacizumab]] (Avastin), was approved by the FDA, as a treatment for colon cancer.  It is a [[recombinant protein|recombinant]] humanized [[monoclonal antibody]] that was discovered and developed by [[Napoleone Ferrara]], a scientist at [[Genentech]].<ref name=NYT2004>Andrew Pollack for the New York Times. February 27, 2004 [https://www.nytimes.com/2004/02/27/business/fda-approves-cancer-drug-from-genentech.html F.D.A. Approves Cancer Drug From Genentech]</ref><ref name=Saga>{{cite journal |vauthors=Ribatti D |title=Napoleone Ferrara and the saga of vascular endothelial growth factor |journal=Endothelium |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=1–8 |year=2008 |pmid=18568940 |doi=10.1080/10623320802092377 }}</ref> A similar drug, [[Lucentis]], was later approved for treating macular degeneration.<ref name=RememberingCHB/> After further work was done by Celgene and others, in 2006 the U.S.&nbsp;Food and Drug Administration granted accelerated approval for thalidomide in combination with dexamethasone for the treatment of newly diagnosed [[multiple myeloma]] patients.<ref name=Beilenberg/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cancer.gov/cancertopics/druginfo/fda-thalidomide|publisher=National Cancer Institute|access-date=January 8, 2012|title=FDA Approval for Thalidomide|archive-date=January 28, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120128120343/http://www.cancer.gov/cancertopics/druginfo/fda-thalidomide|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Awards==
Folkman was a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]], the [[Institute of Medicine]], the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, and the [[American Philosophical Society]], among others. He was the author of some 400 papers and more than 100 book chapters and monographs and received scores of United States awards and honors for his research as well as numerous international awards, including the [[George Ledlie Prize]] from Harvard, Canada's [[Gairdner Foundation International Award]], Israel's [[Wolf Prize]], Germany's [[Ernst Christian Friedrich Schering|Ernst Schering Prize]], the United Kingdom Society for Endocrinology's Dale Medal in 2000,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.endocrinology.org/about/medals/SfEpastMedalists.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130516204243/http://www.endocrinology.org/about/medals/SfEpastMedalists.pdf|url-status=dead|title=Society for Endocrinology Medal Winners|archive-date=May 16, 2013}}</ref> [[Prince of Asturias Award]], the Golden Plate Award of the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]]<ref>{{cite web|title= Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement |website=www.achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration}}</ref> and Switzerland's Dr. Josef Steiner Cancer Research Award.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.steinerstiftung.unibe.ch/guidelines.aspx|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111129115915/http://www.steinerstiftung.unibe.ch/guidelines.aspx|url-status=dead|title=The Dr. Josef Steiner Cancer Research Foundation|archive-date=November 29, 2011}}</ref> In 2005 he was awarded the [[Grand Prix scientifique de la Fondation Lefoulon-Delalande|Scientific Grand Prize of the Lefoulon-Delalande Foundation]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://lefoulon-delalande.institut-de-france.fr/historique-0#12_le_grand_prix_scientifique_2005|title=Historique|date=April 12, 2012|work=Fondation Lefoulon-Delalande Institut de France|access-date=December 12, 2017}}</ref> 

He was awarded the [[Massry Prize]] from the [[Keck School of Medicine]], [[University of Southern California]] in 1997.
On May 29, 1998, Folkman received an [[Honorary degree|honorary doctorate]] from the Faculty of Medicine at [[Uppsala University]], Sweden<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.uu.se/en/about-uu/traditions/prizes/honorary-doctorates/|title=Honorary doctorates – Uppsala University, Sweden|first=David|last=Naylor|website=www.uu.se|date=June 9, 2023 }}</ref>

==Death and legacy==

Folkman died of a heart attack in Denver on January 14, 2008, at the age of 74 en route to deliver the 2008 Keynote Address at the [[Keystone Symposia]] (Molecular Mechanisms of Angiogenesis in Development and Disease) in [[Vancouver, British Columbia]].<ref name=NYTObit>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/01/16/us/16folkman.html|title=Judah Folkman, Researcher, Died at 74 on January 15, 2008|last=Pollack|first=Andrew|date=January 16, 2008|work=The New York Times|access-date=April 11, 2010}}</ref>

He was survived by his wife, Paula, whom he met and married while doing his surgical residency,<ref name=NASbio/> two daughters, and a granddaughter.<ref name=NYTObit/>
